cards.front: In the simple steady-state model of body temperature, write the heat balance using M, G, C, E, body temperature and air temperature.
cards.back: M + G = C × (Tb − Ta) + E: heat made plus heat gained equals the dry leak plus heat evaporated.
cards.quote: heat made (M) + heat gained (G) = conductance (C) × (body temperature − air temperature) + heat evaporated (E)

cards.front: In the steady-state heat balance model, body temperature sits above the air by {{c1::(M + G − E) ÷ C}}.
cards.back: An animal steers its temperature by changing one of those terms.
cards.quote: So body temperature sits above the air by (M + G − E) ÷ C.

cards.front: In the heat balance model, what is conductance (C), and in what units?
cards.back: How readily heat leaks out per degree of body-to-air difference, in watts per kelvin (a kelvin of difference equals a degree Celsius).
cards.quote: conductance is how readily heat leaks out per degree of body-to-air difference

cards.front: What is metabolic rate, and why is the resting metabolic rate treated as M, heat made, in the heat balance?
cards.back: Energy used per unit time, in watts (J per s) or kJ per day. Nearly all of it ends up as heat, so at rest it is M.
cards.quote: Metabolic rate is the energy an animal uses per unit time, in watts (joules per second) or kilojoules per day

cards.front: Name the four routes of heat exchange between an animal and its surroundings, and what carries each.
cards.back: Radiation (electromagnetic energy), conduction (surfaces in contact), convection (moving air or water) and evaporation (whose price is water).
cards.quote: radiation (electromagnetic energy), conduction (surfaces in contact), convection (moving air or water) and evaporation
cards.section: Routes and dials the first film left out

cards.front: How do vasoconstriction and vasodilation of the small arteries to the skin change heat loss, and which term of the heat balance do they change?
cards.back: Constriction keeps warm blood in the core; dilation delivers heat to the surface. Both change conductance C, as do posture, huddling, fur, feathers and blubber.
cards.quote: Narrowing the small arteries to the skin (vasoconstriction) keeps warm blood in the core; widening them (vasodilation) delivers heat to the surface
cards.section: Routes and dials the first film left out

cards.front: How does countercurrent exchange in a bird's leg or a seal's flipper save heat?
cards.back: Warm blood going out passes its heat to cold blood coming back, so the heat returns to the core instead of leaking from the foot.
cards.quote: warm blood going out passes its heat to cold blood coming back, so the heat returns to the core instead of leaking from the foot
cards.section: Routes and dials the first film left out

cards.front: In terms of the heat balance, what distinguishes an endotherm from an ectotherm?
cards.back: An endotherm (mammal, bird) warms itself mainly with M, held in by a low C. An ectotherm takes its temperature mainly from Ta and G.
cards.why: Either can use both sources, and the mix shifts with activity and weather.
cards.quote: An endotherm, such as a mammal or bird, warms itself mainly with M, held in by a low C
cards.section: Endotherms, ectotherms and a second axis

cards.front: What do homeotherm and heterotherm describe, and why is this a separate axis from endotherm and ectotherm?
cards.back: How constant body temperature is: a homeotherm holds it nearly constant, a heterotherm lets it vary widely. Endotherm and ectotherm name the main heat source instead.
cards.quote: A homeotherm holds a nearly constant body temperature, and a heterotherm lets it vary widely.
cards.section: Endotherms, ectotherms and a second axis

cards.front: A small bird keeps its body warm with its own metabolic heat by day, but each night lets its body temperature fall far below the daytime level. Place it on both thermal axes.
cards.back: A heterothermic endotherm.
cards.why: Its main heat source is its own M (endotherm); how constant its temperature stays is the separate axis, and here it varies widely (heterotherm), like a hibernating ground squirrel.
cards.quote: A deep-sea fish in steady cold is a nearly constant ectotherm; a hibernating ground squirrel, whose temperature can fall to near freezing, is a heterothermic endotherm.
cards.section: Endotherms, ectotherms and a second axis

cards.front: Invented iguana model: E = 0, C = 0.05 W per K, M = 0.02 W, surroundings 30 degrees C. Find its steady body temperature with sunshine worth G = 0.48 W, and with no sun.
cards.back: Tb − Ta = (M + G − E) ÷ C. With sun: 0.50 ÷ 0.05 = 10 K, so 40 degrees C. No sun: 0.02 ÷ 0.05 = 0.4 K, so about 30.4 degrees C.
cards.why: With G gone, the ectotherm's small M cannot hold it above the air; a mouse's large M, held in by fur, keeps it near 37 degrees C.
cards.quote: sunshine worth G = 0.48 W holds it at 40 degrees C in 30 degree surroundings; with no sun it settles toward 30.4 degrees C
cards.section: Endotherms, ectotherms and a second axis

cards.front: In mammals, where is the temperature controller, and what does it compare its sensor signals against?
cards.back: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus. It weighs skin and core sensor signals against its set point, the temperature it aims for.
cards.quote: The controller, centred in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus, weighs these signals against its set point, the temperature it aims for
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: In mammalian thermoregulation, contrast feedback and feed-forward responses.
cards.back: Feedback starts when the core moves away from its defended range (as in exercise). Feed-forward starts from skin sensors before the core has changed.
cards.quote: Feed-forward responses start from the skin before the core has changed
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: In the cold, in what order does a mammal typically deploy its responses?
cards.back: Behaviour first (seek warmth, huddle), then narrowing of skin arteries and extra heat production.
cards.why: Behaviour tends to come before the costlier physiological responses.
cards.quote: Behaviour tends to come before the costlier physiological responses.
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: How do humans, horses, dogs, many birds and rodents each cool by evaporation?
cards.back: Humans and horses sweat; dogs and many birds pant; rodents spread saliva on their fur.
cards.quote: humans and horses sweat, dogs and many birds pant, and rodents spread saliva on their fur
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: Why does shivering produce heat rather than movement?
cards.back: Opposing muscles contract involuntarily and rhythmically at the same time, so little external work is done and the energy appears as heat.
cards.quote: involuntary, rhythmic contraction of opposing muscles at the same time, so little external work is done and the energy appears as heat
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: How does UCP1 in brown adipose tissue mitochondria turn food energy into heat?
cards.back: UCP1 lets protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane, so the energy becomes heat instead of ATP.
cards.quote: UCP1, which lets protons leak back across the inner membrane so food energy becomes heat instead of ATP
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: A mouse lacking UCP1 is moved into cool air. Which ways remain for it to raise heat made (M) or cut heat loss?
cards.back: Shivering still raises M, and behaviour (huddling, seeking warmth) and skin vasoconstriction still lower C. Only the UCP1 brown-fat route to M is lost.
cards.why: Two responses raise M, shivering and brown fat, and the same controller switches on both.
cards.quote: Many mammals also have brown adipose tissue, whose mitochondria carry the protein UCP1
cards.section: Sensing and control: what the controller does

cards.front: Under what conditions is basal metabolic rate (BMR) measured?
cards.back: In an endotherm that is awake, resting, postabsorptive (not digesting a meal) and within its thermoneutral zone.
cards.quote: measured in an endotherm that is awake, resting, postabsorptive (not digesting a meal) and within its thermoneutral zone
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: What is an endotherm's thermoneutral zone?
cards.back: The range of air temperatures over which it spends no extra energy on heating or cooling.
cards.quote: the range of air temperatures over which it spends no extra energy on heating or cooling
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: An invented mouse-like endotherm has body temperature 37 degrees C, BMR 0.25 W and minimum conductance 0.035 W per K. Calculate its lower critical temperature.
cards.back: Lower critical temperature = Tb − BMR ÷ Cmin = 37 − 0.25 ÷ 0.035 = 37 − 7.1, about 29.9 degrees C.
cards.why: The bend falls where the conductance needed to shed exactly BMR reaches the minimum the animal can set.
cards.quote: lower critical temperature = Tb − BMR ÷ Cmin = 37 − 0.25 ÷ 0.035, about 29.9 degrees C
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: The same invented endotherm (Tb 37 degrees C, BMR 0.25 W, minimum C 0.035 W per K, no sun, evaporation neglected) sits in 21 degree C air. How much heat must it make, as a multiple of BMR?
cards.why: Below its minimum conductance it cannot hold the leak to BMR, so it must make more heat.
cards.quote: Inside the animal's range, it stays basal; below its minimum, it must make more heat.
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: A researcher reports a laboratory mouse's metabolic rate, measured at a room temperature of 21 degrees C, as its basal metabolic rate. What is wrong with the label?
cards.back: 21 degrees C is below the mouse's thermoneutral zone (measured near 29 to 33 degrees C), so the rate includes the cost of making heat. BMR must be measured within the thermoneutral zone.
cards.quote: so animal rooms near 20 to 22 degrees C are cool for a mouse
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: An invented endotherm (Tb 37 degrees C, BMR 0.25 W) can open its conductance to at most 0.10 W per K. Above what air temperature can dry heat loss alone no longer shed its BMR?
cards.back: Gap needed = BMR ÷ Cmax = 0.25 ÷ 0.10 = 2.5 K, so above about 37 − 2.5 = 34.5 degrees C. Evaporation must grow, or body temperature must rise.
cards.quote: even the widest C, 0.10 W per K, can shed BMR only across a gap of 2.5 K
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: What marks the upper critical temperature of the thermoneutral zone?
cards.back: The air temperature where active heat loss, such as panting, starts to raise metabolic rate.
cards.why: It is not the same as the dry model's threshold where dry loss alone falls short; the simple model leaves out the cost of panting.
cards.quote: the upper critical temperature, where active heat loss such as panting starts to raise metabolic rate
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: An arctic fox and a tropical mammal have the same basal rate and a body temperature near 37 degrees C (round illustrative numbers). The fox's lower critical temperature is near −40 degrees C, the tropical animal's near +27 degrees C. How many times lower is the fox's minimum conductance?
cards.back: BMR = Cmin × (Tb − lower critical temperature). Gaps are about 77 K and 10 K, so the fox's Cmin is about 77 ÷ 10, roughly 7 to 8 times lower.
cards.quote: The gaps are about 77 K and 10 K, so the fox's Cmin is roughly 7 to 8 times lower.
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: In a shaded chamber the air and walls are both at 40 degrees C, above a mouse's 37 degrees C body temperature. Which term of the heat balance can still carry heat out, and how much must it remove?
cards.back: Only evaporation. The dry leak has turned negative, so E must remove the metabolic heat plus all the heat radiation, conduction and convection bring in.
cards.quote: Only evaporation. With the whole surroundings at 40 degrees C, the dry leak has turned negative
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: Invented numbers: an endotherm holds 37 degrees C with constant C = 0.030 W per K, below its lower critical temperature. The air falls from 27 to 17 degrees C. Find the extra heat production, the extra energy per day, and the fat burned (fat yields about 39 kJ per g).
cards.back: Extra power = 0.030 × (27 − 17) = 0.30 W. Per day: 0.30 J per s × 86,400 s = 25,920 J = 25.9 kJ. Fat: 25.9 ÷ 39 = about 0.66 g per day.
cards.quote: Assume fat yields about 39 kJ per g.
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: An endotherm at 37 degrees C with constant C = 0.020 W per K must make 0.40 W at 17 degrees C air. It fluffs its fur and halves C. What must it make now?
cards.back: 0.20 W: 0.010 W per K × 20 K. Halving conductance halves the cost at the same temperature gap.
cards.why: Heat made = C × (Tb − Ta). A 10 degree cooling does not generally double metabolism; that only happens when C is fixed and the gap doubles.
cards.quote: Fluff the fur so C falls to 0.010 W per K, and the cost at 17 degrees C drops back to 0.20 W.
cards.section: The cost of keeping warm: numbers on the curve

cards.front: At the start of a fever the target temperature rises from 37 to 39 degrees C while the body is still at 37. Does the patient feel hot or cold, and what does the body do?
cards.back: Cold. Body temperature is below the new target, so the controller acts as if chilled: it conserves heat and makes more, for example by shivering, until it reaches 39.
cards.quote: Body temperature is now below the target, so the controller acts as if the body were chilled
cards.section: Fever, torpor and hibernation: changing the target

cards.front: In mammals, how does an infection raise the temperature the brain defends?
cards.back: Infection signals lead cells lining brain blood vessels to make prostaglandin, which acts on the brain's temperature-control region and raises the defended temperature.
cards.quote: signals from an infection lead the cells lining brain blood vessels to make prostaglandin, which acts on the brain's temperature-control region
cards.section: Fever, torpor and hibernation: changing the target

cards.front: A feverish mammal is steady at a raised 39 degrees C. It is given a drug that blocks prostaglandin synthesis, and the defended temperature returns to 37. What happens next, and why?
cards.back: It now feels warm and runs heat-loss responses: skin vessels widen, then evaporation (sweating or panting, depending on species) until the body cools to 37.
cards.why: Fever is regulation at a raised level set by prostaglandin; with the target lowered, the body is above its set point, so the controller runs its heat-loss responses.
cards.quote: Fever is regulation of body temperature at a raised level.
cards.section: Fever, torpor and hibernation: changing the target

cards.front: Define torpor and daily torpor.
cards.back: Torpor is a controlled drop in metabolic rate and body temperature in a bird or mammal. Daily torpor conventionally lasts under 24 hours.
cards.quote: Torpor is a controlled drop in metabolic rate and body temperature in a bird or mammal.
cards.section: Fever, torpor and hibernation: changing the target

cards.front: Contrast hibernation in small hibernators such as ground squirrels with hibernation in black bears.
cards.back: Ground squirrels: torpor bouts of days to weeks, body temperature can fall to near freezing, broken by costly periodic arousals. Black bears: about 30 to 36 degrees C for months, no periodic arousals.
cards.quote: Black bears hibernate differently: body temperature stays at roughly 30 to 36 degrees C for months, with no periodic arousals.
cards.section: Fever, torpor and hibernation: changing the target

cards.front: A mouse moved into cool air narrows its skin vessels and makes extra heat before its core temperature falls. Design an experiment to tell skin sensing apart from core and brain sensing.
cards.back: Change one site's temperature while holding the others steady, recording skin blood flow and heat production. Cool the skin with the core kept warm; then warm or cool the preoptic area alone with skin and air steady.
cards.why: If skin sensing drives the response, vessels narrow and heat production rises even with a warm core.
cards.quote: Cool the skin while keeping the core warm: if skin sensing drives the response, the skin vessels narrow and heat production rises anyway.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mice with the gene for the cold sensor TRPM8 disrupted keep core temperature in a broadly normal range. Does this show TRPM8 plays no part in thermoregulation?
cards.back: No. The system has several overlapping inputs that largely compensate, so a normal temperature after a knockout does not rule out a role for the sensor.
cards.quote: A normal body temperature after a knockout does not show that the sensor plays no part.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What is standard metabolic rate (SMR), and why must its temperature be stated?
cards.back: The ectotherm's equivalent of BMR: resting, postabsorptive, at a stated temperature, because an ectotherm's rate changes with temperature.
cards.quote: Standard metabolic rate (SMR) is the ectotherm's equivalent of BMR: resting, postabsorptive, and at a stated temperature
cards.section: Measuring metabolic rate: conditions and scaling

cards.front: How does daily energy expenditure differ from basal metabolic rate?
cards.back: Daily expenditure is everything over 24 hours: activity, digestion, heating, growth. Exercise adds to it but is not part of BMR, measured at rest.
cards.quote: The work of exercise adds to it but is not part of BMR, which by definition is measured at rest.
cards.section: Measuring metabolic rate: conditions and scaling

cards.front: Across mammals and birds, how does whole-body BMR scale with body mass, and what does that mean per gram?
cards.back: BMR rises more slowly than body mass, so a gram of mouse spends far more than a gram of elephant. The exponent is a fitted value, and its cause is unsettled.
cards.quote: whole-body BMR rises more slowly than body mass, so a gram of mouse spends far more than a gram of elephant
cards.section: Measuring metabolic rate: conditions and scaling

cards.front: Why can the steady-state heat balance not describe a lizard warming on a morning rock completely?
cards.back: The lizard is storing heat, so the balance gives only where its warming curve levels off, not how fast it gets there.
cards.quote: A lizard warming on a morning rock is storing heat, so the steady-state balance gives only where its warming curve levels off, not how fast it gets there.
cards.section: Where the balance stops: stored heat

cards.front: Most fish cannot keep their bodies warm, yet the opah warms its whole body. Using the countercurrent principle, explain why the opah's heat exchangers sit in the gills.
cards.back: In most fish, blood leaving the gills is cooled to water temperature. In the opah, countercurrent exchangers between arteries carrying blood into and out of the gills keep fin-muscle heat in the body.
cards.why: Same rule as a bird's leg: outgoing warm blood passes heat to returning cold blood, so heat returns to the core.
cards.quote: so blood leaving the gills is not cooled all the way to water temperature as in most fish
cards.section: Who described the opah

cards.front: Infected desert iguanas held each at one fixed temperature (34 to 42 degrees C) survived better when warmer. Bacterial growth in culture was similar from 34 to 40 degrees C. What does the culture result suggest, and what does it leave open?
cards.back: Warmth likely helped through the host's defences rather than by directly harming the bacteria, but the host change was not identified, and the result does not transfer automatically to mammals or other infections.
cards.quote: The paper's own test of bacterial growth in culture found it similar from 34 to 40 degrees C
cards.section: Fever: the evidence in detail

cards.front: Illustrative numbers: a black bear's metabolic rate falls to 25% of basal as its body temperature falls from 37 to 33 degrees C. Assuming Q10 = 2.5, how much of the fall could cooling alone explain?
cards.back: Predicted fraction = 2.5^(−4/10) = 2.5^(−0.4) = 0.69. Actual 0.25 ÷ 0.69 = 0.36 is left unexplained, so most of the fall is active suppression, not cooling.
cards.why: The Q10 of 2.5 is an assumption; there is no universal Q10.
cards.quote: The bear is at 25%, so a further factor of 0.25 / 0.69 = 0.36 is left unexplained by temperature
cards.section: Is hibernation just cooling? A worked estimate

cards.front: What measurement separates passive cooling from active metabolic suppression in a hibernating black bear, and what did it show?
cards.back: Record oxygen consumption and body temperature together, continuously, through hibernation and emergence. Metabolism stayed low for up to three weeks after body temperature returned to normal, so it did not simply follow temperature.
cards.quote: In the real bears it stayed low for up to three weeks after body temperature had returned to normal
cards.section: Is hibernation just cooling? A worked estimate
